source.title: Scaling Proprioceptive-Visual Learning with Heterogeneous Pre-trained Transformers
source.authors: Lirui Wang; Xinlei Chen; Jialiang Zhao; Kai-Ming He

record.tranche_reason: The study investigates scaling and transfer in heterogeneous robot-policy pretraining, a different model and training setting from language-model scaling.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy. Its pretraining metric is validation action-prediction error using a Huber loss. Rows record reported robot-policy scaling results and downstream transfer results; these do not establish language-model power laws or a compute-optimal parameter/token split.
record.test_reason: The study runs robot-policy (HPT) pretraining sweeps over data, model size, batch size and dataset count, and reports validation action-prediction loss. This is a new-setting check of whether loss scaling carries beyond text (V5). It fits no power law, and every loss result is figure-only, so it can only bear on V5 qualitatively.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim HPT scales 'to some extent' with data quantity and diversity, model size and compute, as measured by validation loss. They report that pretrained representations improve transfer in simulation and the real world and correlate with pretraining performance. They call their scale moderate and the validation-loss metric caveated.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses supervised robot-policy pretraining and Huber action-prediction validation loss, rather than language-model pretraining and held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies dataset quantity and diversity, model size, batch size/training samples, and added simulation or human-video data. It also notes that the averaged validation metric depends on the evaluation subset and on how many training steps each dataset receives.

fits_no_version.finding: Downstream robot transfer success rises modestly with pretrained trunk size and lower pretraining loss: HPT-XL 76.7±3.3% vs HPT-B 70.0±3.0% on Sweep Leftover. The authors say transfer 'shows correlations with pre-training performance'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In robot-policy pretraining, downstream transfer success improves with trunk scale and pretraining validation loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding simulation and human-video datasets to pretraining is feasible, and the authors say these datasets are complementary.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-domain heterogeneous data can be added to robot-policy pretraining without harming validation loss.

record.problems: The study does not fit power laws or report numerical loss values for the scaling plots in the text. It says validation loss depends on the evaluation subset and training steps, and that validation loss and downstream closed-loop task performance can diverge. Its authors describe the data and compute scale as moderate.

Language-model shape at fixed parameter count. Only a one-line robot-policy depth vs width remark appears.
The power-law form itself: no fit and no exponents. Image/video generative models, repeated data and LM fine-tuning are also untested.

All of it: no fits and no comparison of published laws.

missing.what: Model-scaling sweep: 'We do not find a significant difference between scaling depth or scaling width' (robot-policy analogue of shape insensitivity; no numbers).
Blue line in Fig. 7: model scaling with fixed data and epochs, without the compute increase. This is the bottlenecked comparison to R4.
Transfer-learning loss improves with pretrained model size (model size ablation in loss curves).

record.verdict_notes: Loss here is Huber action-prediction error, not LM cross-entropy. All scaling results are figure-only, with no fitted laws. V6 rows were unlinked because the version concerns language-model downstream performance. The reader's V6 labels are dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger language-model runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its scaling with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count in language models.

The study tests robot-policy pretraining with heterogeneous data, but does not fit or establish a power-law form. It does not test image/video models as such, repeated-data training, or other listed regimes.
The study reports robot-policy transfer performance, not language-model downstream task predictability; it does not establish a predictive law relating pretraining loss to downstream performance.

It does not fit exponents, compare compute-optimal allocations, or test the stated disagreements between published language-model laws. It does discuss how validation-set selection and training steps can affect its robot-policy validation metric.

rows.subject: HPT-S
rows.size_stated: 3.17 million parameters in the default setting
rows.operation_detail: Varied trajectory count while keeping training iterations fixed.

conditions.value: maximum 10 to 100000 per dataset; 270 to 170k total

rows.value: figure only; text says fixed-iteration HPT-S can plateau at around 1000 trajectories maximum per dataset
rows.note: The text attributes the early plateau to increasing data while other factors, including compute, remain bottlenecks.
rows.check: This is HPT-S at fixed iterations, with data scaled while compute is held fixed. The plateau falls under a bottleneck that V5/V1 explicitly exclude, so it cannot show presence or absence of the effect.

rows.subject: HPT scaling runs (Figure 5(a), red line)
rows.size_stated: larger model; exact sizes not stated for this series
rows.operation_detail: Scaled trajectory count together with model size and batch size.

conditions.value: batch size doubled for each order-of-magnitude increase in trajectory count

rows.value: figure only; text reports better validation losses as total trajectory count increases
rows.note: The text reports a scaling trend but gives no fitted power law or numerical loss values.
rows.check: Subject should be HPT-L, which per the Fig. 5(a) caption is trained with 4x more tokens than HPT-S. Loss improves with trajectories, but there is no power-law fit or numbers, so the form is untested.

rows.subject: HPT-S through HPT-XL
rows.size_stated: HPT-S to HPT-XL; exact sizes not assigned to individual plotted results in the text
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of training datasets.

conditions.value: fixed subset of the first 10 datasets

rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviations across 4 runs are plotted; numerical values not stated
rows.note: The authors hypothesize that training with more embodiments contributes to trunk generalization, but the text does not state the plotted loss trend.
rows.check: The text does not state the direction of the loss trend over dataset count, and this axis is data diversity rather than a parameter, token or compute axis.

rows.subject: HPT model-scaling runs (Figure 7, red line)
rows.operation_detail: Scaled model size while increasing data and training compute to approach convergence.

conditions.value: 256 to 2048, doubling for each order of model-size increase

rows.value: figure only; text says larger models with more compute achieve low validation losses until plateau
rows.note: The text describes improvement and a plateau, but does not give numerical losses or fit a power law.
rows.check: Loss falls with model size (1M to 1B) only 'until it is plateaued'. No fit or values are given.

rows.subject: HPT-S
rows.operation_detail: Increased batch size, thereby increasing training samples/tokens seen.
rows.value: figure only; text says increasing batch size/training tokens generally improves performance until convergence
rows.note: The left plot varies batch size; the right derives the relationship using batches seen multiplied by samples per batch.
rows.check: Loss improves with samples seen 'until convergence'. This is figure-only, with no functional form.

rows.subject: HPT pretraining with simulation and human-video data
rows.operation_detail: Compared the default dataset mixture with mixtures adding simulation and human-video datasets.

conditions.value: default setting without simulation and human datasets

rows.note: The text says pretraining on additional embodiment datasets is possible and that they provide complementary data, but does not state the plotted loss differences.
rows.check: This compares data mixtures (adding simulation and human video) against the default mix. It is not a scaling sweep along parameters, tokens or compute, and no plotted difference is stated.

rows.subject: HPT-Base Finetuned
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated the fine-tuned policy on the Sweep Leftover real-world task.
rows.note: This is a downstream robot-policy result, not language-model performance.
rows.check: A single model's success rate is not a scale comparison. It also concerns robot-policy transfer, not the language-model downstream predictability that V6 names. It is best used only as the baseline for R8.

rows.subject: HPT-XL Finetuned
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated the fine-tuned policy on the Sweep Leftover real-world task.
rows.note: The larger fine-tuned model has higher reported success on this task.
rows.check: HPT-XL vs HPT-B on Sweep Leftover (76.7±3.3 vs 70.0±3.0) is a two-point robot-policy comparison, not language-model downstream performance. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: HPT-B through HPT-XL transfer models
rows.stage_stated: pretrained trunks transferred to downstream simulation tasks
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream task success for transferred models across simulator benchmarks.

conditions.value: reported as plotted results in Figure 10(a)

rows.value: figure only; text reports improved success rates using pretrained models ranging from HPT-B to HPT-XL
rows.uncertainty: 5 independent training runs and evaluations were averaged for each model
rows.note: The text reports an overall improvement with pretrained models; individual task values are not given in the text.
rows.check: Robot-policy simulator transfer is figure-only. The text is ambiguous on whether improvement is across sizes or relative to from-scratch baselines. Moved to fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Heterogeneous robot-policy pretraining (HPT, 1M–1B trunk), Huber action-prediction validation loss
relationships.reason: Loss falls with data, model size and samples seen but plateaus. No power-law fit is reported, and the authors say HPT scales only 'to some extent' (R2, R4, R5).
relationships.display_finding: Huber action-prediction loss fell with data, model size, and samples seen before plateauing, without a fitted power law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Heterogeneous robot-policy pretraining with Huber action-prediction validation loss
reader_labels.reason: The reported sweeps show improvement in some data/model/compute settings, plateaus, and a dataset-count result whose direction is not stated; no power-law fit or exponent is reported (R1-R6).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Sweep Leftover real-world transfer and the reported simulator transfer trend
reader_labels.reason: The larger HPT-XL has higher Sweep Leftover success than HPT-Base, and the authors report improved simulation success using pretrained models across the tested size range (R7-R9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The results are limited to robot-policy transfer, with one exact two-size comparison and no stated predictive relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance (R7-R9).
